explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. "A gentle answer turns away wrath…" and the heat leaves the room. The angry person still has feelings, but nobody tossed fresh logs on the fire. Soft words are a quiet kind of strong.

I get the pull, friend, because we ALL want to be right. But the verse never says a gentle answer wins the argument. It says it "…turns away wrath…" Cooling a room down and winning a debate are two different jobs, and the first one is the one this verse hands you.

Close, but the verse says nothing about the talking stopping. What leaves is the wrath: "A gentle answer turns away wrath…" I think a calm reply actually gives a conversation room to keep going. Two people can't work anything out while one of them is a smoking oven.

You got it, baker! The verse says, "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good." No spot is left out, not even a quiet corner. The verse puts no limit on where. And what He observes is both the evil and the good.

The temple is a fine place to think of, but the verse doesn't draw a fence like that. It says, "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good." Every place is a BIG list, friend. That leaves nothing out.

Jerusalem is one specific place, but the verse doesn't name any city at all. It says, "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good." That covers Jerusalem and everything outside it too.

You got it, baker. The verse says "…a perverse tongue crushes the spirit." Look at the two sides of it: a soothing tongue is a tree of life, and a perverse one flattens a person. Words are heavier than they look.
Refreshing is the soothing tongue's job, friend. That's the tree of life half of the verse. The perverse tongue does the opposite and crushes the spirit.

Guarding sounds nice, but it isn't in this verse. Here the perverse tongue doesn't protect anybody's spirit, it crushes it. Picture a cookie under a rolling pin that's way too heavy. That's crumbs, not protection, and the verse says "…a perverse tongue crushes the spirit."
Nailed it, baker. "…whoever heeds correction is prudent." Prudent just means careful and wise. The person who listens when somebody says "hey, try it this way" ends up on the smart side of the verse.

Stubborn is the other side of the verse, friend. The one who rejects discipline is called a fool. The one who heeds correction is called prudent. I've been stubborn at the baking counter, and the cookies let me know about it.

A lot of us feel that way about taking correction, like it's admitting defeat. But the verse says the opposite: whoever heeds correction is prudent. Listening to correction is called wise, not weak. Swallowing your pride is a strong move.

Careful, baker, this one flips at the end. The verse says "The lips of the wise spread knowledge, but not so the hearts of fools." Fools don't spread knowledge the way the wise do. Only half of that sentence was true.
That's right, friend. The verse says "The lips of the wise spread knowledge, but not so the hearts of fools." Knowledge-spreading belongs to the wise side. The fool's heart doesn't do it.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is His delight." Look at who's holding what: a sacrifice is something you bring, a prayer is something you say, and the verse says the one who brings it matters. Plot twist, right? Then verse 9 says it about whole lives: "The LORD detests the way of the wicked, but He loves those who pursue righteousness."
Pleasing belongs to the other half, friend. The prayer of the upright is His delight. The sacrifice of the wicked is called detestable.

I see the thinking, but the verse doesn't leave it hanging. The sacrifice of the wicked isn't unknown to the LORD, it's detestable to Him. And right after, the prayer of the upright is His delight. The verse says plainly where each one lands.
That's right, baker. "…He loves those who pursue righteousness." Notice the word pursue, which means they're chasing it. And the LORD loves the ones who go after it.
Testing isn't in this verse, friend. It says "The LORD detests the way of the wicked, but He loves those who pursue righteousness." The word for the ones chasing righteousness is love.
Warning is a fair thing to expect, since this chapter has plenty of correction in it. But this verse is about love. "…He loves those who pursue righteousness." Same verse, warm ending.

Hold on, baker, the verse ends the other way. It says "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD…" and then adds, "…how much more the hearts of men!" If those deep places are open before Him, hearts are open too. They aren't hidden.

Right, friend. The verse says, "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD—how much more the hearts of men!" Those two lie open before Him. So the "…how much more…" tells you hearts are no harder for Him to see. Nothing in there is hidden from Him.

That's it, baker. "A joyful heart makes a cheerful countenance…" Countenance is just a fancy word for your face. What's going on inside tends to show up on the outside, like when I smell a fresh batch and my whole mustache lifts.
Money does show up in this chapter, friend, but not in this verse. Here it says "A joyful heart makes a cheerful countenance…" The joy goes straight to the face, no bank involved.
A long life sounds great, but this verse doesn't promise it. It says "A joyful heart makes a cheerful countenance…" So what a joyful heart makes is a cheerful face.

Yes, baker. The verse says "All the days of the oppressed are bad, but a cheerful heart has a continual feast." It puts the two side by side. I'd take the continual feast, and I'm saying that as a guy with a whole bakery.
That one's true, friend. The verse sets the hard days of the oppressed next to a cheerful heart that "…has a continual feast." Continual means it keeps going. It doesn't run out.

That's it, baker. The verse says, "Better a dish of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred." A fattened ox is a fancy meal, and it still loses to a plain dish with love at the table. The verse calls the dish of vegetables where there is love the better one.
Hunger sounds like the natural opposite of a fattened ox. But in this verse the ox is already on the table. The problem comes with it: hatred. Vegetables where there is love beat it.
Sorrow shows up in this chapter, friend, but not in this verse. Here it's "…a fattened ox with hatred." The meal is great and the company is the trouble.

Right, baker. The verse says, "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger calms dispute." One person adds fuel and the other takes it away. The verse puts them side by side, and the results go opposite ways. Being slow to anger is quiet work, but it does calm things down.
Actually, friend, that one's true. The verse says "…he who is slow to anger calms dispute." The hot-tempered man stirs up strife, and the slow-to-anger one calms it. The two sit on opposite sides.

Watch the second half, baker. The verse says "A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish man despises his mother." So the foolish man doesn't honor her, he despises her. The first half you had right.
That's right, friend. "A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish man despises his mother." The question swapped in "honors," but the verse says despises. That's a big difference in one word.
Yes, baker, and it's a sneaky one. "Folly is joy to one who lacks judgment…" Someone without judgment actually enjoys the silly choices. Meanwhile the man of understanding walks a straight path.
Grief isn't the word in this verse, friend. It says, "Folly is joy to one who lacks judgment…" The one lacking judgment finds joy in it. Meanwhile the man of understanding walks a straight path.
Shame isn't the word the verse uses, friend. It says, "Folly is joy to one who lacks judgment…" He enjoys it. The man of understanding is the one walking the straight path.

Yes, baker! The verse says, "Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed." It puts failure on the side of lacking counsel and success on the side of many advisers. So the verse points you toward asking around. One more voice in the kitchen never hurt a batch.
Asking around can feel slow, I'll give you that. But the verse isn't talking about timing. It says "…with many advisers they succeed." The result is success, not delay.
That's the first half of the verse, friend. "Plans fail for lack of counsel…" is where that comes from. The second half gives the other result: "…with many advisers they succeed."
That's right, baker. "The path of life leads upward for the wise, that he may avoid going down to Sheol." Up for the wise, and the verse sets that against going down. The direction matters.

Backward is a fun guess, friend, but the verse picks a different direction. It says, "The path of life leads upward for the wise…" Then it mentions going down to Sheol. So the picture is up against down.
Outward isn't a direction the verse uses. It says the path of life leads upward for the wise. Then it mentions going down to Sheol, so the picture is up versus down.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but He protects the boundaries of the widow." A widow is a woman whose husband has died. The verse says it's her boundaries He protects. The proud get their house torn down, and she gets her boundaries protected.
A king is a fair guess, friend, but the verse names someone else. It says, "The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but He protects the boundaries of the widow." The one named is the widow.
I see the thinking, friend, but this verse isn't about priests. It says the LORD tears down the house of the proud, but protects the boundaries of the widow. She's the one named.

Hold on, baker, the verse reaches wider than that. It says, "He who is greedy for unjust gain brings trouble on his household…" The trouble lands on the whole house, not just the one chasing the money. So the verse doesn't leave the household out of it.
That's right, friend. The verse says "He who is greedy for unjust gain brings trouble on his household…" So it isn't only on himself. The whole house feels it.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked blurts out evil." The righteous heart does its thinking first. That's the opposite of blurting.
Waiting your turn is a nice habit, friend, but it isn't what the verse says. It says "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer…" The righteous heart is busy thinking about the answer.

Staying silent is a different thing from what the verse describes. It says, "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer…" The heart is pondering how to answer, not going quiet. The wicked mouth blurts, and the righteous heart thinks.

That's right, baker. The verse says, "The LORD is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous." That's a heavy line, and the verse doesn't soften it. Then it turns on a dime to the prayer of the righteous. I'd rather be on the hearing side of that verse.

Close to isn't what the verse says, friend. It says, "The LORD is far from the wicked…" So close to flips the first half around. The word for the righteous is hears: "…He hears the prayer of the righteous."
Kind is a gentler word, but it isn't the one the verse uses. It says "The LORD is far from the wicked…" Then the verse turns to the righteous, whose prayer He hears.
That one's flipped on you, baker. The verse says "He who ignores discipline despises himself…" Ignoring discipline isn't protecting yourself. It's the opposite.

Right, friend. The verse says, "He who ignores discipline despises himself, but whoever heeds correction gains understanding." Ignoring discipline doesn't protect him. The verse puts the two side by side. The one who heeds correction gains understanding.

Yes, baker! The chapter closes with "The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom, and humility comes before honor." Humility is named first and honor comes after it. Honor doesn't get to cut the line. That's the order the verse sets.
Wealth isn't in this last line, friend. It says, "…humility comes before honor." Wealth gets no spot in that sentence. The chapter ends with humility going first.
Victory has a nice ring to it. But the verse says "…humility comes before honor." Humility is what comes first, and victory isn't mentioned.
